newsitem.title: GERMANY: Georgia returns German books seized as war booty.
newsitem.headline: Georgia returns German books seized as war booty.

text.p: Georgia on Wednesday returned a treasure trove of rare books to Germany half a century after the invading Red Army took them away after World War Two, closing another chapter in Bonn's reconciliation with its former foes.

Originally seized as war booty, nearly 100,000 volumes, some dating back to the 15th century and including priceless Martin Luther editions, were given to Georgia by the Soviet State Fund for Literature in 1947.

"The books returning home today are invaluable German cultural property," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said at a ceremony at the Berlin State Library. "We are thrilled they are returning to their home libraries."

Most of the books survived without significant damage after almost half a decade's slumber in the cellar of the main library of the Georgian Academy of Sciences and other smaller libraries in the former Soviet republic.
Their return to Germany was based on a cultural accord agreed by the two countries in 1993 and ratified by Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze in January of this year.
Last month Ukraine, another former Soviet republic courting Germany as a donor and investor for its creaking economy, pledged to return all the seized German works of art it holds.

Georgian ambassador Konstantin Gabashvili took the chance on Wednesday to claim some credit for his country, telling Kinkel: "No one should believe that these books could not have found use in Georgia, but we wanted the building of our statesmanship to begin with good deeds."

The bulk of the books, works of art and manuscripts seized by the Soviet Union from Nazi Germany, including the legendary golden hoard of ancient Troy, are now in Russia, which has shown much less desire to cooperate.
Moscow argues the treasures are legitimate booty taken from a defeated enemy which surrendered unconditionally.
Kinkel took the opportunity to remind Russia of Germany's wishes.

"Respect for the law, the dignity and the culture of our neighbours is a matter of course in the partnership that we are looking for," he said. "We also want to straighten out our relations with Russia on that basis.
"For that we need patience and sensitivity. But the burdens of history should not be allowed to weigh us down anew."
